{"id": "18:28/q27", "question": "What ancillary argument is made about the Quran's inimitability?", "turns_on": "Whether proof rests on opponents' failure or an expert but undefined sense of eloquence.", "positions": [{"id": "18:28/q27/p1", "position": "The open challenge to produce any sura and opponents' failure show inability to match the Quran.", "reasons": "Khattabi says specifying no sura exposes an inadequate explanation; Baqillani argues opponents had motive, time and argumentative skill (43:58, 19:97, 16:4), yet offered shifting charges (8:31, 28:36, 15:6, 21:3, 37:36, 25:4-8, 15:91), war and demands for signs."}, {"id": "18:28/q27/p2", "position": "Its inimitability lies in eloquence whose ranks skilled ears recognize though its cause is hard to define.", "reasons": "Khattabi reports speculative scholars and followers, then rejects the undefined impression as leaving ignorance untreated. Narrators' Jarir-Dhu al-Rumma story illustrates crafted eloquence."}]}
{"id": "18:28/q28", "question": "How does 'be patient with yourself' state the object of patience?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:28/q28/p1", "position": "The self is stated explicitly as the object of 'be patient', though this object is often omitted in such constructions.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari, as reported by Burhan, says sabara ʿan omits 'the self', whereas 18:28 states it explicitly."}]}
{"id": "18:45/q01", "question": "Whom does the command to give this parable address?", "turns_on": "Whether the address is tied to the wealthy opponents in the preceding passage, Meccans more broadly, deniers of the world's end, or all people.", "positions": [{"id": "18:45/q01/p1", "position": "Arrogant wealthy people who preferred their possessions to poor believers.", "reasons": "Muqatil identifies Meccan unbelievers; al-Tabari, al-Tha'labi, al-Qurtubi and al-Tabrisi connect them with the demand to expel devoted poor believers (18:28). Al-Razi specifies wealthy polytheists boasting of wealth and supporters. Islahi describes people blinded by worldly love; Kuranyolu adds pride in sons, denial of monotheism and the claim that only worldly life exists (68:14–15; 45:24). Al-Asamm connects the command to the preceding passage."}, {"id": "18:45/q01/p2", "position": "The Prophet's people or the people of Mecca generally.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas says the Prophet's people; al-Asamm relates an identification with the people of Mecca."}, {"id": "18:45/q01/p3", "position": "People denying that worldly life will end.", "reasons": "Al-Asamm relates this identification among the alternative addressees."}, {"id": "18:45/q01/p4", "position": "Everyone living in this world.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i says the image applies to worldly life for everyone."}]}
{"id": "18:45/q02", "question": "What condition of worldly life does the parable portray?", "turns_on": "Whether the image chiefly represents rapid loss of beauty, the coexistence of pleasure and harm, or the world's remarkable condition.", "positions": [{"id": "18:45/q02/p1", "position": "Its beauty and flourishing rapidly give way to decay and disappearance.", "reasons": "Muqatil connects the fading world with the Hereafter's arrival. Yahya, al-Zajjaj, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, al-Kashshaf, Ibn Atiyya, al-Tabrisi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Razi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, Ibn Kathir, al-Biqa'i, Bursevi, al-Alusi, Elmalili and al-Tabataba'i trace fresh rain-fed growth into dry windblown fragments. Al-Zajjaj, al-Kashshaf, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and al-Alusi say the vanished growth is as though it never existed. Ibn Ashur maps youth, prosperity, novelty and adornment onto rain, growth and dispersed loss; the shared turn from good to bad makes an abstract state visible. Al-Razi compares 22:5, where earth stirs and swells. Kashifi compares youth to a tree dried by death and hopes blown away. Islahi cites 57:20 on amusement, adornment and rivalry in wealth and children. Al-Burhan says the rain-and-growth simile makes the short duration of the world's bloom visible in greenery that soon disappears."}, {"id": "18:45/q02/p2", "position": "Its blessings are inseparable from adversity, and joy from grief.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi gives this as an alternative purpose. Al-Qushayri says worldly pleasures conceal sorrow, sweetness bitterness, gifts trials, and promises fail. Ibn al-Jawzi lists changing fortunes and grief paired with joy as an alternative reading."}, {"id": "18:45/q02/p3", "position": "The world has a remarkable condition worthy of a parable.", "reasons": "Al-Baydawi allows the world's extraordinary quality as the object of comparison; al-Alusi reports the command as explaining that remarkable condition."}]}
{"id": "18:45/q03", "question": "Why is worldly life compared specifically to water?", "turns_on": "Whether water's own properties supply the likeness or the whole plant cycle does.", "positions": [{"id": "18:45/q03/p1", "position": "Both change location and condition and cannot be retained.", "reasons": "The sages reported by al-Tha'labi and al-Qurtubi say neither remains fixed; al-Burhan adds that water slips from a closed hand."}, {"id": "18:45/q03/p2", "position": "Both eventually disappear.", "reasons": "The sages in al-Tha'labi say water vanishes as worldly life ends; al-Qurtubi transmits the same comparison."}, {"id": "18:45/q03/p3", "position": "Contact with either brings unavoidable effects and trials.", "reasons": "The sages say one cannot enter water without becoming wet, just as worldly life exposes one to harms and trials."}, {"id": "18:45/q03/p4", "position": "A sufficient amount benefits, while excess harms or destroys.", "reasons": "The sages in al-Tha'labi and al-Qurtubi contrast useful provision with damaging surplus; al-Burhan repeats this analogy."}, {"id": "18:45/q03/p5", "position": "The comparison is to the entire rain, growth, decline and dispersal scene.", "reasons": "Al-Burhan calls this the fuller comparison. Bursevi and al-Alusi explicitly reject restricting the likeness to water alone; Ibn Ashur analyzes the shared passage from prosperity to loss as a composite simile."}]}
{"id": "18:45/q04", "question": "How is كَمَآءٍ attached grammatically?", "turns_on": "The valency of اضرِب and whether the kāf starts an independent explanation, supplies a second object, or modifies an omitted verbal noun.", "positions": [{"id": "18:45/q04/p1", "position": "It begins an explanatory clause with an omitted subject: worldly life is like water.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi and Ibn Atiyya supply the omitted subject. Abu Hayyan and al-Samin transmit Ibn Atiyya's parse. Al-Alusi prefers this fresh explanation and objects that a second object of ḍaraba is awkward. Bursevi explains the comparison in these terms."}, {"id": "18:45/q04/p2", "position": "It is the second object of اضرِب: make the likeness resemble water.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan prefers this parse. Al-Samin prefers it because ḍaraba can mean ṣayyara and credits al-Baqa with the proposal. Al-Baydawi also permits water as a second object."}, {"id": "18:45/q04/p3", "position": "It modifies an omitted verbal noun: strike a likeness in a manner like water.", "reasons": "Al-Hawfi assumes aḍrib takes one object and supplies ḍarban; Abu Hayyan and al-Samin report him. Al-Alusi rejects this analysis."}]}
{"id": "18:45/q05", "question": "What is the water sent from the sky?", "turns_on": "The sources distinguish the water's identity from the range of meanings of السماء.", "positions": [{"id": "18:45/q05/p1", "position": "Rain.", "reasons": "Al-Tha'labi and al-Wahidi identify the water as rain. Al-Biqa'i says it descends by God's power at the needed time. Al-Tabataba'i says rain is named because other water sources begin with it. Al-Samin parses أَنزَلْنَٰهُ as an adjective of water."}, {"id": "18:45/q05/p2", "position": "Sky can mean a cloud or the direction above.", "reasons": "Bursevi gives both possible senses of heaven in the phrase."}]}
{"id": "18:45/q06", "question": "What happens in فَٱخْتَلَطَ بِهِۦ نَبَاتُ ٱلْأَرْضِ, and what does ب do?", "turns_on": "Whether the plants mix with one another because of rain or the water itself mixes into the plants, with a corresponding causal or participant sense of ب.", "positions": [{"id": "18:45/q06/p1", "position": "Plants become abundant and intertwine with each other because of the water; ب marks cause.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi, al-Wahidi, al-Kashshaf, Ibn Atiyya, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, Bursevi, al-Alusi and Ibn Ashur give the dense-growth account. Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Ashur explicitly call the bā' causal; Ibn Ashur denies that it makes ikhtalaṭ transitive. Al-Samin allows cause and cites al-Zamakhshari. Al-Razi says rain strengthens and entangles kinds of plants. Al-Biqa'i includes water mingling with soil and producing varied dense growth."}, {"id": "18:45/q06/p2", "position": "Water mingles with and saturates the plants until they flourish; ب can mark the other participant in mixing.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi gives this alternative. Abu Ishaq in al-Wahidi says water penetrates the plants. Al-Asamm, the Kashshaf's alternative, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, al-Samin and al-Alusi describe saturation; al-Kashshaf, al-Razi and al-Samin say either of two mixed things can be grammatically described as mingling with the other. Al-Samin also allows transitivity for ب."}]}
{"id": "18:45/q07", "question": "Why does the wording make vegetation mix with water?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:45/q07/p1", "position": "The reversal emphasizes abundant water and luxuriant growth.", "reasons": "Al-Baydawi and al-Alusi observe that ordinary phrasing would make water mix with plants; the verse makes water seem the dominant mass. Al-Tabataba'i says the wording highlights rain's role in forming the vegetation."}]}

{"id": "18:45/q09", "question": "Does أَصْبَحَ mean became or literally became by morning?", "turns_on": "Whether morning is an actual temporal detail or أَصْبَحَ functions as a general verb of becoming.", "positions": [{"id": "18:45/q09/p1", "position": "It means became, with no necessary morning time.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya cites a line by Rabi' b. Dab' for a resultant state; al-Samin cites poetry too. Al-Alusi says the verse describes eventual drying. Ibn Ashur calls this common usage; al-Tabataba'i denies a morning restriction."}, {"id": "18:45/q09/p2", "position": "It may mean that the plant became dry by morning.", "reasons": "Al-Samin notes that calamities commonly strike in the morning. Al-Alusi reports the literal-morning account as motivated by heavenly calamities arriving at night, but says only eventual drying is described."}]}
{"id": "18:45/q10", "question": "What does the فَ before أَصْبَحَ convey?", "turns_on": "Whether the conjunction marks swift change directly or telescopes an unspoken period of growth.", "positions": [{"id": "18:45/q10/p1", "position": "It conveys how quickly flourishing growth vanishes.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports this reading of the immediate sequence."}, {"id": "18:45/q10/p2", "position": "It resumes the account after an omitted period of flourishing.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports an explanatory fā' with a time interval understood. Al-Mawardi notes that the water's absence before drying is implicit for concision."}]}
{"id": "18:45/q11", "question": "What does هَشِيمًا mean and how is it formed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:45/q11/p1", "position": "Dry, broken or crumbled vegetation and other fragile matter.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba derives it from hashama, breaking, and relates Hashim's name. Al-Tha'labi transmits Ibn Abbas's dry, al-Dahhak's broken and al-Akhfash's crumbled glosses. Al-Mawardi says drying and breaking, with a poem comparing dead bodies to dried plants; water's disappearance is tacit. Al-Wahidi compares crumbling bread and Hashim's name. Al-Jishumi adds broken hollow things; al-Kashshaf gives hashimah as singular. Ibn Atiyya compares tharid and 54:31. Ibn al-Jawzi transmits al-Farra's formerly moist and al-Zajjaj's dry definitions. Al-Razi cites an anonymous line about crushing bread. Al-Qurtubi lists dry wood and extended uses for generosity, weakness, affection, camel milking and crumbled bread; Ibn al-Ziba'ra's verse and the account of Hashim feeding Mecca after famine explain his name. Abu Hayyan and al-Samin report the former-moist definition; al-Samin calls hashim the singular of hashimah. Al-Alusi permits intensive passive or plural of hashimah; Ibn Ashur gives fa'il with passive force; Bursevi says the root breaks something soft."}]}
{"id": "18:45/q12", "question": "What action does تَذْرُوهُ describe?", "turns_on": "The glosses emphasize dispersal, turning motion, or lifting; al-Qurtubi says their senses are close.", "positions": [{"id": "18:45/q12/p1", "position": "The wind scatters, casts or blows the plant fragments away.", "reasons": "Al-Farra compares forms from dharā and adhrā and cites al-Mufaddal's poem about casting off; al-Majaz, Ibn Qutayba and al-Tabari give the basic scatter sense, while al-Tabari's anonymous line uses yadhruk for throwing someone from a mount. Abu Ubayda, al-Qutaybi and later transmitters gloss scattering and blowing. Al-Wahidi gives several dialect forms and dispersal; al-Jishumi says tadhriya scatters light objects in every direction. Ibn Atiyya cites 54:31; al-Qurtubi cites a Sibawayh and al-Farra verse about wind blowing a bird off course and says the glosses are close. Abu Hayyan notes dharā and adhrā as paired forms. Bursevi compares winnowing grain; Ibn Ashur says dharw is throwing into the air. Al-Damghani glosses dharw as wind-driven scattering or dispersal and mentions 51:1 as supporting usage."}, {"id": "18:45/q12/p2", "position": "The wind carries the fragments to and fro or turns and stirs them.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas and Ibn Kaysan give turning and back-and-forth motion in al-Tha'labi; al-Baghawi reports Ibn Abbas's stirring. Al-Qurtubi treats these as close to scattering. Abu Hayyan, al-Alusi and al-Tabataba'i transmit the back-and-forth gloss; al-Biqa'i combines stirring with dispersal. Al-Nahhas transmits al-Farra's related adhraytu for turning a person on a camel."}, {"id": "18:45/q12/p3", "position": "The wind lifts or raises the plant debris.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash gives this gloss in al-Tha'labi, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi; al-Wahidi includes lifting among the motions, and al-Samin also reports it."}]}
{"id": "18:45/q13", "question": "What is the syntactic role of تَذْرُوهُ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:45/q13/p1", "position": "It is an adjective describing the broken vegetation.", "reasons": "Al-Samin explicitly parses the verb phrase as a modifier of hashim."}]}
{"id": "18:45/q14", "question": "How is تَذْرُوهُ read?", "turns_on": "Attested recitations use related wāw and yā' roots and different verb forms, with named readers and vowels varying among reports.", "positions": [{"id": "18:45/q14/p1", "position": "The common reading is تذروه from the wāw form.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas labels it the common reading; al-Zajjaj says two other forms are possible in Arabic but not recited. Al-Farra and al-Majaz give variant verb forms with comparable scattering sense."}, {"id": "18:45/q14/p2", "position": "A reading has تذريه, with forms derived from the alternate yāʾ or causative verb.", "reasons": "Al-Farra attributes tadhrihi al-rih to Abdullah; al-Nahhas adds a report from al-Kisa'i. Al-Tha'labi assigns scattering or lifting forms to Talha b. Musarrif; al-Jishumi calls Talha's form a dialect variant. Al-Wahidi and Abu Hayyan cite Ibn Mas'ud. Ibn Atiyya cites Ibn Abbas; al-Kashshaf reports Ibn Abbas's causative form. Ibn al-Jawzi lists Ubayy, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Abi Abla with raised tā', kasra on rā' and silent yā'; Ibn Mas'ud differs with fatḥa on tā'. Al-Samin separates Abdullah's yā' radical from Ibn Abbas's ḍamma tā' causative reading, perhaps derivable from either root. Al-Qurtubi gives Talha and Ibn Mas'ud; al-Alusi calls Ibn Mas'ud's form quadriliteral."}]}
{"id": "18:45/q15", "question": "Is ٱلرِّيَٰحُ read in the plural or singular?", "turns_on": "Reader attribution and the connotation of singular versus plural wind.", "positions": [{"id": "18:45/q15/p1", "position": "Plural الرياح is the common reading.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj gives the plural. Al-Nasafi attributes it to Hamza and Asim; Abu Hayyan and al-Samin call it the majority form. Al-Kashshaf reports a plural-winds reading of Ibn Abbas with a causative verb."}, {"id": "18:45/q15/p2", "position": "Singular الريح is also read.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya names al-Hasan and others; al-Qurtubi reports Talha's tadhrihi al-rih. Abu Hayyan notes several authorities. Al-Samin names Zayd b. Ali, al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i; al-Alusi additionally lists al-A'mash, Talha, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Muhaysin, Khalaf, Ibn Isa and Ibn Jarir. Qiraat-Er associates singular rih in classical usage with destructive wind."}]}
{"id": "18:45/q16", "question": "How is مُقْتَدِرًا formed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:45/q16/p1", "position": "It is on the iftaʿala pattern from q-d-r.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba and Ibn al-Jawzi give the derivation."}]}
{"id": "18:45/q17", "question": "What does كَانَ convey about God's power?", "turns_on": "Whether past kāna states an eternal or precreation attribute, or can point to future power without a tense-shifting cue.", "positions": [{"id": "18:45/q17/p1", "position": "His power is timeless or has always existed, including before creation.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj prefers Sibawayh and al-Khalil: kāna describes timeless power, and Arabic past tense cannot mean future or present without a shifting particle. Al-Nahhas reports some saying always and prefers Sibawayh's explanation that observed power was already God's. Al-Wahidi reports al-Zajjaj that power was not newly acquired; Ibn Atiyya transmits Sibawayh's rationally recognized prehuman power and al-Hasan's precreation state. Al-Tabrisi follows al-Zajjaj and Sibawayh. Al-Biqa'i calls divine power eternal, not newly acquired. Al-Nahhas reports Abu Ishaq's rejection of an unsignalled future sense."}, {"id": "18:45/q17/p2", "position": "He was able to bring all things into being before they existed.", "reasons": "Al-Hasan gives the precreation explanation in al-Zajjaj, al-Wahidi and al-Tabrisi; Ibn Atiyya also reports him. It specifies the pre-existing scope of divine ability."}, {"id": "18:45/q17/p3", "position": "The past form may mean He will be or is and will be powerful.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj reports the kā'in wa-yakūn interpretation but argues it conflicts with ordinary tense usage. Al-Nahhas reports the future sense. Al-Tabrisi reports using past power to point toward future events."}]}
{"id": "18:45/q18", "question": "What does God's being مُقْتَدِرًا encompass here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:45/q18/p1", "position": "Power over all things, especially creating, sustaining, ending and restoring life.", "reasons": "Muqatil includes resurrection; al-Tabari applies power to ruining gardens and worldly wealth. Al-Zajjaj and al-Wahidi name origination and annihilation; al-Wahidi argues from God's producing and ending vegetation. Al-Kashshaf, al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi, Ibn Kathir, Bursevi, al-Alusi and al-Biqa'i name creation and destruction; al-Qurtubi and al-Biqa'i include restoration or enlivening. Al-Razi adds nurturing before abolition. Al-Thalabi and al-Baghawi state universal power. Yahya and Elmalili conclude God can do all things. Islahi sees power in both producing and decaying worldly luxuriance."}]}

{"id": "18:45/q20", "question": "How does this parable relate to other Quranic parables and verses?", "turns_on": "The cited verses illuminate different parts of the same growth-and-loss image.", "positions": [{"id": "18:45/q20/p1", "position": "It condenses or parallels the water-and-vegetation parable of 10:24.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi calls this a shortened version and points to his fuller explanation in Yunus; Ibn al-Jawzi says the comparison is elaborated there. Bursevi calls it a condensation. Ibn Kathir also cites 10:24."}, {"id": "18:45/q20/p2", "position": "Other verses also picture temporary growth that withers or worldly adornment that passes.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir cites 39:21 and 57:20 plus an authentic hadith calling the world sweet and green. Al-Alusi cites 87:4–5, where pasture becomes dark dry debris. Islahi uses 57:20 to explain worldly amusement and rivalry. Study Quran cites 39:21 and 57:20; al-Razi cites 22:5 for the rain-fed earth stirring and swelling."}, {"id": "18:45/q20/p3", "position": "A parallel rain-to-greening passage illustrates the sequence behind this parable: the resulting greening may follow by consequence, ordinary succession, or immediately once its causes are complete.", "reasons": "Ibn Malik, as reported by al-Burhan, treats the present-tense result after rain as consequential, while an alternative supplies omitted stages of growth and greening. Ibn al-Hajib, as reported there, allows customary sequence even when years intervene. Another account reported by al-Burhan takes greening as immediate once its causes are complete. Al-Burhan also explains that the present tense after the particle need not be subjunctive: the preceding question confirms rather than genuinely asks, and rain itself, rather than seeing it, causes greening."}]}
{"id": "18:45/q21", "question": "How does the verse connect with the surrounding garden story and its aftermath?", "turns_on": "The sources look either backward to the garden story or forward to the contrast with lasting deeds.", "positions": [{"id": "18:45/q21/p1", "position": "It extends the lesson of the ruined garden and the failure of pride in wealth.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari links the address to 18:28 and garden boasting to 18:36. Bursevi says the brother's admonition failed because the listener's heart hardened and ended in regret. Study Quran says verses 32–44 show dependence on divine beneficence and the garden's final barren plain. Al-Nahhas transmits Abu Ishaq's allowance of the preceding verse's ʿuqbā on the pattern of bushrā and a poetic tazlaq line from Sibawayh and al-Mufaddal; these are lexical details in the nearby garden context."}, {"id": "18:45/q21/p2", "position": "The next lesson contrasts passing ornaments with enduring righteous deeds.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya says righteous work remains in the afterlife while worldly beauty and power fade. Islahi says ornaments do not accompany people to the next world; Kuranyolu contrasts transient wealth and children with enduring righteous deeds."}]}
{"id": "18:45/q22", "question": "What conduct does the parable call for toward worldly goods?", "turns_on": "Whether the ethical emphasis is avoiding pride and misplaced reliance, limiting consumption, or using worldly life without attachment.", "positions": [{"id": "18:45/q22/p1", "position": "Do not boast in or rely on passing wealth; seek the enduring afterlife and righteous deeds.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari warns against pride in wealth and urges work for the Hereafter. Al-Razi says inevitable decline makes delight in worldly beauty unreasonable. Ibn Atiyya, Bursevi and al-Alusi turn the cycle toward reliance on lasting deeds rather than adornment; Bursevi uses Saadi's images of aging, a worm-eaten royal shroud and returning spring. Al-Biqa'i adds worldly toil and anxieties. Islahi says luxury, status and possessions engross the affluent; Kuranyolu says wealth and children pass and condemns using blessings for arrogance or pressure against the poor."}, {"id": "18:45/q22/p2", "position": "Use sufficient worldly provision with contentment, avoiding harmful excess.", "reasons": "The sages' water comparison distinguishes a useful measure from destructive surplus. Al-Qurtubi reports a saying to take from the world like still water, where little suffices and much intoxicates, and a Muslim report that success is submission, sufficiency and contentment."}, {"id": "18:45/q22/p3", "position": "Worldly life can be gain for the discerning when used without attachment.", "reasons": "Wahb's account in Bursevi contrasts discerning gain with ignorant heedlessness and says prophets and saints lived in the world without clinging to it."}]}
{"id": "18:45/q23", "question": "Which prophetic sayings are cited about living in the world?", "turns_on": "The reports highlight sufficiency and contentment or the world's initial attractiveness.", "positions": [{"id": "18:45/q23/p1", "position": "Take from the world like still water: a little suffices and much intoxicates.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi reports this as the Prophet's reply to a man asking to be among the successful."}, {"id": "18:45/q23/p2", "position": "Success belongs to one who submits, receives sufficiency and is made content.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi attributes this prophetic report to Muslim."}, {"id": "18:45/q23/p3", "position": "The world is sweet and green.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir mentions an authentic hadith alongside related Quranic parables."}]}
{"id": "18:45/q24", "question": "What inward meaning is drawn from the rain and vegetation?", "turns_on": "The inward reports map the image to the lower self, the growth of faith, and the role of grace in spiritual ascent.", "positions": [{"id": "18:45/q24/p1", "position": "Divine care joins spirit to body, while prophetic teaching sows faith in the heart.", "reasons": "Bursevi makes water and earth stand for spirit and body; prophets and saints plant faith and monotheism in fertile hearts through invitation, nourished by the Law. He cites 14:24; the good word and action raise the spirit toward divine nearness (35:10)."}, {"id": "18:45/q24/p2", "position": "The spirit's outcome depends on God's grace and attraction.", "reasons": "Bursevi says God may leave the spirit in animal-like corporeality or draw it to the highest nearness, where angels prostrate. He cites Jami that years of a seeker's effort alone do not attain the beloved without attraction."}, {"id": "18:45/q24/p3", "position": "Worldly adornment is what the lower self continually inclines toward.", "reasons": "Muhammad b. al-Fadl, as transmitted by al-Sulami, calls the world the lower self's close companion, drawing it through inward and outward decoration."}]}
{"id": "18:45/q25", "question": "How is مُقْتَدِرًا connected to the reported gloss of مُقِيت?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:45/q25/p1", "position": "A transmitted gloss gives مُقِيت the sense capable, echoing مُقْتَدِرًا here.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shati says muqit occurs only in 4:85 and its root relates to sustenance, alongside aqwāt in 41:10; she cites a reported Quraysh usage meaning qādir and a supporting line by al-Zubayr b. Abd al-Muttalib."}]}
{"id": "18:46/q01", "question": "What do wealth and sons signify in worldly life?", "turns_on": "Whether the focus is their attractiveness, their practical support, or their testing and danger.", "positions": [{"id": "18:46/q01/p1", "position": "They are attractive but transient worldly adornments, unable by themselves to provide lasting benefit or indicate divine favor.", "reasons": "Muqatil contrasts their fleeting beauty with afterlife reward. Al-Tabari, al-Tha'labi, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Kathir, al-Biqa'i, al-Alusi, Ibn Ashur, Tabataba'i, Islahi, Kuran Yolu, and Study Quran stress that they perish and cannot furnish the grave. Study Quran cites 18:34, 17:6, 18:7–8; Ibn Kathir cites 3:14 and 64:15. Al-Tabari illustrates rich men boasting over Salman, Khabbab, and Suhayb. Ibn Ashur cites Tarafa's poem as evidence of Arab pride in property and noble sons."}, {"id": "18:46/q01/p2", "position": "Wealth supplies beauty, benefit and livelihood; sons supply strength, defense, family continuity and public status.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi distinguish wealth's beauty and benefit from sons' power and protection. Islahi explains Arabian tribal backing and displays of numbers. Study Quran calls them status and security. Al-Biqa'i adds that either may benefit if used to please God, or harm and disappoint."}, {"id": "18:46/q01/p3", "position": "Wealth and children are a test and may even become enemies or a means of distance from God.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi cites 64:15 and 64:14. Ibn Kathir cites 64:15. Bursevi invokes verses on apparent increase and a divine report, with 23:55–56, saying abundance may distance a believer whereas restriction brings nearness."}]}
{"id": "18:46/q02", "question": "Why is wealth named before sons?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:46/q02/p1", "position": "Wealth is the more fundamental, immediately needed ornament and support.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi says it benefits parents and children at all times, while sons aid only parents; wealth sustains an individual and can adorn without sons, whereas sons without wealth may bring distress."}, {"id": "18:46/q02/p2", "position": "Arabic ordering puts a singular before a plural: singular wealth therefore precedes sons, whereas plural heaps of wealth would follow sons.", "reasons": "The author of al-Burhan explains the order by the Arabic practice of placing a singular befor

{"id": "18:46/q03", "question": "What does zīna mean here and in related Qur'anic uses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:46/q03/p1", "position": "It is what beautifies something and makes it desirable; here it includes worldly display or luxury.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi defines adornment by its attraction to the self and distinguishes its Qur'anic senses: general beauty (2:212, 3:14, 67:5), jewelry (20:87), luxury or wealth (10:88 and this verse), and a public retinue such as Qarun's finery (28:79)."}]}
{"id": "18:46/q04", "question": "How does the singular zīna predicate wealth and sons?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:46/q04/p1", "position": "Zīna is a verbal noun used for the two concrete subjects, by emphasis or with an omitted description.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya notes that a description must be supplied, though the excerpt ends before giving it. Al-Samin says they are themselves adornment emphatically, or things that adorn. Abu Hayyan permits an omitted possessor or taking the pair as abundance. Al-Alusi says the verbal noun is transferred to the adorned thing. Al-Qurtubi permits singular and dual predicates."}]}
{"id": "18:46/q05", "question": "Is zīna read in another number?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:46/q05/p1", "position": "A rare reading has dual zīnatā al-ḥayāh.", "reasons": "Al-Samin says its alif drops in pronunciation before the next consonant cluster, making the form resemble an accusative singular; al-Qurtubi says the dual is grammatically possible."}]}
{"id": "18:46/q06", "question": "Why are wealth and sons called adornment of worldly life?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:46/q06/p1", "position": "The genitive confines their adornment to this quickly decaying life.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi allows either ornaments belonging specifically to worldly life or ornaments found in it; if that life rapidly decays, its ornaments decay even sooner. {"id": "18:46/q07", "question": "Whose boasting does the verse address?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:46/q07/p1", "position": "It rebukes rich unbelieving leaders who boasted over poor believers.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari names Uyayna and al-Aqra against Salman, Khabbab, and Suhayb; al-Tha'labi, al-Wahidi, and al-Qurtubi name Uyayna and his peers. Al-Baghawi calls the leader Utba. Abu Hayyan, al-Razi and Ibn Ashur identify wealthy polytheists; Kuran Yolu calls them wealthy Meccans rejecting monotheism. {"id": "18:46/q08", "question": "What occasion is reported for this passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:46/q08/p1", "position": "The passage beginning with the command to recite revelation is linked to Uyayna and al-Aqra's treatment of poor worshippers.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari says the section from 18:27 through this verse was revealed about them; al-Suddi relays Khabbab's account beginning with the order not to drive away those calling on God morning and evening (6:52)."}]}
{"id": "18:46/q09", "question": "What are the enduring righteous deeds?", "turns_on": "Whether named devotions define the entire phrase or exemplify the general class; al-Tabari stresses unrestricted wording, while Sa'id's rejection and al-Alusi's reading of 'these are' support restriction.", "positions": [{"id": "18:46/q09/p1", "position": "Every act or word of obedience whose reward God preserves, including the named forms of worship and remembrance.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari prefers the unrestricted wording because Scripture and Prophetic reports do not exclude other works; the report says four phrases are among the deeds. Al-Zajjaj, al-Tabrisi, al-Qurtubi and the reported choice of Ibn Jarir agree. Ibn Abbas lists prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, charity, emancipation, jihad and kinship; al-Tha'labi adds testimony, forgiveness and blessings on the Prophet. Al-Razi includes deeds leading to knowledge, love and service. Al-Baydawi names Ramadan fasting and good speech; Kuran Yolu includes faith, moral conduct, enjoining good and kindness. Tabataba'i treats specific reports as examples. Al-Alusi reports al-Khafaji's inclusion argument but questions whether Prophetic 'these are' permits it. Al-Itqan cites Ibn Jarir's report from Abu Hurayra in which the Prophet calls the four formulas 'among' the lasting good deeds, leaving the class unrestricted."}, {"id": "18:46/q09/p2", "position": "The five prescribed daily prayers.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Amr ibn Shurahbil, Ibrahim, Abu Maysara, Masruq and Ibn Mas'ud are named in various chains. Al-Tha'labi and al-Durr connect them with 11:114, where good deeds erase bad ones. Yahya also reports a combined view attributed to Ibn Abbas, taking prayers and formulas together. Al-Damghani also mentions 19:76 when identifying the deeds as the five daily prayers."}, {"id": "18:46/q09/p3", "position": "The four formulas of glorifying, praising, affirming God's oneness and magnifying Him.", "reasons": "Muqatil and several transmitters cite Prophetic identifications; Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrima, Dahhak, Hasan and Qatada also give this list. Al-Ghazali, as quoted by al-Razi, reads them as ascending knowledge: freedom from defect, source of good, oneness, and greatness beyond reason. Abu Hurayra's report says they are 'among' the enduring deeds. Ibn al-Jawzi also reports an Ali formula substituting reliance for glorification or praise; it varies slightly. Reports on these formulas' merits appear separately below. Al-Itqan gives a second report from Abu Saʿid identifying the four formulas, and a similar raised report transmitted by al-Ṭabarānī from Saʿd ibn Junadah."}, {"id": "18:46/q09/p4", "position": "The four remembrance formulas together with lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi-llāh.", "reasons": "Uthman, Ibn Umar, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Ata, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Prophetic reports give the fivefold list. Some transmitted lists vary: Abu Sa'id's list omits explicit praise in al-Tha'labi; Ibn Umar and Ali lists also vary. Sa'id explicitly rejects prayer, fasting, almsgiving and pilgrimage as the specific answer. Abraham's Paradise planting report supports inclusion of hawqala; Salim challenges then accepts Muhammad ibn Ka'b's addition. Ibn Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan call this the majority interpretation. Abd al-Haqq graded one report sound. Al-Itqan transmits Abu Saʿid's Prophetic report listing all five formulas, including praise of God and the statement that there is no might or power except through God."}, {"id": "18:46/q09/p5", "position": "Good speech or words of goodness.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas is reported through al-Awfi and others; al-Razi cites 22:24 about the people of Paradise. Al-Wahidi says good speech is itself remembrance. Al-Baydawi includes it alongside worship."}, {"id": "18:46/q09/p6", "position": "Sincere intentions or actions done purely for God's approval.", "reasons": "Ibn Ata and al-Hasan say intentions make actions accepted and raised. Al-Sulami also reports sincere acts; al-Qushayri requires truthfulness and absence of self-seeking; Qatada and al-Biqa'i emphasize seeking God's face. Al-Alusi reports love, knowledge, intimacy, sincere tawhid and turning from others as an inward form."}, {"id": "18:46/q09/p7", "position": "Righteous daughters, or reward for raising daughters well.", "reasons": "Ubayd ibn Umayr reads a contrast with sons; al-Qurtubi cites Aisha's poor mother and daughters, a report of daughters pleading for their father at Hell, and Qatada's account of the daughter promised at 18:81 who bore twelve prophetic sons. Bursevi cites a Prophetic shield-from-Fire promise for good care. A bereaved parent may count a child as an enduring reward, as al-Durr's burial and bereavement reports illustrate."}, {"id": "18:46/q09/p8", "position": "Love of the Prophet's family.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi transmits Abu Abd Allah telling al-Husayn ibn Abd al-Rahman that their love is among the enduring deeds; Tabataba'i reports it as an instance."}, {"id": "18:46/q09/p9", "position": "Night prayer specifically.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi reports this from Abu Abd Allah."}, {"id": "18:46/q09/p10", "position": "Divine unity itself.", "reasons": "Al-Sulami reports Ja'far al-Sadiq: tawhid remains as long as its professing believer remains."}, {"id": "18:46/q09/p11", "position": "Sincere counsel to other people.", "reasons": "Al-Sulami reports Yahya ibn Mu'adh's identification."}, {"id": "18:46/q09/p12", "position": "Remembrance of God generally.", "reasons": "The author of al-Itqan identifies the lasting good deeds as remembrance of God without limiting them to a named set of formulas."}]}
{"id": "18:46/q10", "question": "Why are the deeds called enduring and righteous?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:46/q10/p1", "position": "Their reward or fruit remains with God after worldly benefits pass away.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari says each righteous act remains for its doer. {"id": "18:46/q12", "question": "How does bāqiyāt work grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:46/q12/p1", "position": "It qualifies omitted words or deeds, with the enduring reward understood by ellipsis.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi also allows attachment to a deleted noun."}]}
{"id": "18:46/q13", "question": "Why does bāqiyāt precede ṣāliḥāt?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:46/q13/p1", "position": "The reversed expected order stresses permanence against vanishing wealth and sons.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says ṣāliḥāt normally comes first as a noun for good works, citing 18:107 and Jarir's verse; the preceding scattered-plant parable (18:45) supplies the omitted thought that worldly ornaments vanish, while 'enduring' reinforces it. {"id": "18:46/q14", "question": "What does 'better in reward' mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:46/q14/p1", "position": "Righteous deeds yield superior, lasting recompense with God in the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Yahya, al-Tha'labi, al-Mawardi, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, al-Kashshaf, Ibn Atiyya, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, al-Biqa'i, al-Alusi, Ibn Ashur, Tabataba'i, Asad and Islahi contrast certain enduring divine reward with wealth, sons and polytheists' recompense. Al-Razi argues spiritual and intellectual goods exceed sensory ones, and the Hereafter unites both. Al-Alusi says 'with your Lord' may mean in the Hereafter or by God's judgment; al-Durr distinguishes the believer's hope and the polytheist's reward."}]}
{"id": "18:46/q15", "question": "What does thawāb mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether thawāb is glossed as recompense or benefit.", "positions": [{"id": "18:46/q15/p1", "position": "Recompense or reward, from the notion of returning.", "reasons": "Jishumi gives the root explanation; al-Alusi allows reward and recompense. Al-Damghani cites 18:31 in connection with the sense of recompense or reward."}, {"id": "18:46/q15/p2", "position": "Benefit.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports this alternative gloss."}]}
{"id": "18:46/q16", "question": "What does 'better in hope' mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:46/q16/p1", "position": "Righteous deeds are a more reliable and worthy object of hope than wealth and children.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba glosses the best thing one can hope for; al-Wahidi says better than what one hopes from wealth and children. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nasafi contrast failible worldly expectations with God's true promise. Al-Baydawi, al-Biqa'i, Bursevi and al-Alusi say deeds fulfill hopes in the afterlife; Tabataba'i contrasts divine mercy and honor with deceiving worldly hopes. {"id": "18:46/q17", "question": "What does amal mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:46/q17/p1", "position": "Hope or expectation.", "reasons": "Jishumi treats these as near synonyms; Ibn Qutayba explains it as what one hopes for."}]}
{"id": "18:46/q18", "question": "What is the grammar of thawāban and amalan?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:46/q18/p1", "position": "They are accusative specifications distinguishing the two comparisons.", "reasons": "Jishumi gives this parsing."}]}
{"id": "18:46/q19", "question": "How can the verse call the deeds 'better' than worldly adornment?", "turns_on": "Whether the comparison is rhetorical, answers mistaken evaluation, or compares recompenses.", "positions": [{"id": "18:46/q19/p1", "position": "The comparative need not grant genuine goodness to the worldly alternative.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi cites Arabic comparison with an inferior that has no good, including 25:24; al-Qurtubi likewise points to Paradise as a 'better' resting place."}, {"id": "18:46/q19/p2", "position": "The comparison answers what ignorant people merely suppose is good.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi reports the supposition view. Jishumi allows a hypothetical answer to those claiming another can reward, even though God would be best."}, {"id": "18:46/q19/p3", "position": "It compares actual recompenses for different deeds without needing a real divine rival.", "reasons": "Jishumi offers this alternative."}]}
{"id": "18:46/q20", "question": "Why repeat 'better' for reward and hope?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:46/q20/p1", "position": "It emphasizes superiority or marks two distinct grounds for it.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi gives both explanations."}]}
{"id": "18:46/q21", "question": "What do reports say the remembrance formulas accomplish?", "turns_on": "The reports describe different benefits and contexts rather than competing definitions.", "positions": [{"id": "18:46/q21/p1", "position": "They plant trees or other growth in Paradise.", "reasons": "Abu Ayyub's Ascension report has Abraham describe good spacious soil and hawqala as planting; al-Tirmidhi's Ibn Mas'ud report adds sweet water and barren ground, graded hasan gharīb. Ibn Majah reports that each of four formulas plants a tree for its reciter. Muhammad ibn Ka'b's disputed hawqala is confirmed by Salim through Abu Ayyub."}, {"id": "18:46/q21/p2", "position": "They shield from the Fire and aid their reciter on Judgment Day.", "reasons": "Al-Tha'labi and al-Durr report that the formulas surround their reciter; al-Tabrisi and Bursevi report a shield. Al-Qurtubi cites a report graded sound by Abd al-Haqq. Al-Hasan's dream has a voice naming four formulas as protection against fear."}, {"id": "18:46/q21/p3", "position": "They erase sins like leaves falling from a tree.", "reasons": "Al-Tha'labi, al-Qurtubi, al-Durr and al-Alusi cite versions. Al-Tirmidhi calls one gharīb and notes al-A'mash saw but did not hear Anas; Ibn Majah reports a comparable version via Abu al-Darda. They are also called Paradise's treasures."}, {"id": "18:46/q21/p4", "position": "They are urged especially when harder worship or fighting is beyond one's ability.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi reports the Prophet's counsel; Ibn al-Jawzi transmits it via Abu Hurayra. Al-Baghawi's Abu Sa'id report also urges increasing the formulas and gives no grading."}, {"id": "18:46/q21/p5", "position": "They outweigh worldly goods and other sacrifices.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawi reports the Prophet calling them the best words and dearer than all the sun rises over. Al-Durr reports Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas comparing them to the Nile and Euphrates, the Prophet preferring them to equal dinars, and Abd Allah ibn Amr preferring them to bridled battle horses."}, {"id": "18:46/q21/p6", "position": "A night reciter who says each of four formulas a hundred times after ablution is forgiven except for bloodshed.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir cites the report through Sa'd ibn Janadah; another Sa'd report says the Prophet taught him three short suras and the four formulas after his conversion."}, {"id": "18:46/q21/p7", "position": "They bring counted merits and divine remembrance.", "reasons": "Al-Durr reports good deeds and erased bad deeds for particular formulas; a heavenly circuit around the Throne with God's remembrance of their speaker; angels carrying phrases upward and praying for the speaker; and their use as a substitute for someone unable to memorize Qur'an."}, {"id": "18:46/q21/p8", "position": "Four formulas are among five weighty deeds along with patiently losing a righteous child.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir also reports five beliefs leading to Paradise: God, Last Day, Paradise, Hell, resurrection and reckoning; the enumerated beliefs vary in count from the stated five."}, {"id": "18:46/q21/p9", "position": "A report pairs the four formulas with refusal to support or believe unjust rulers.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir gives the account through an unnamed Ansari."}, {"id": "18:46/q21/p10", "position": "A personal report values supplication for guidance and worship above hoarded gold and silver.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir gives Shaddad ibn Aws's regret at asking for a knife to play with, then the Prophetic prayer for steadfastness, gratitude, sound heart, truthful tongue, good, refuge and forgiveness; Ahmad and al-Nasa'i transmit it."}]}
{"id": "18:46/q22", "question": "What larger lesson does the verse draw about worldly attachments?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:46/q22/p1", "position": "Prefer lasting righteous action and hope in the Hereafter to pride or dependence on perishing wealth and family.", "reasons": "Jishumi urges Paradise and detachment because life passes quickly; al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi quote Ali's two harvests, though God may give both. Al-Qurtubi warns that wealth, women and power change hands. Ibn Kathir urges worship rather than endless accumulation or worry. Al-Razi ranks lasting spiritual and intellectual happiness above sensory goods. Al-Biqa'i says worldly possessions fail when most needed. Kuran Yolu disapproves of arrogance and pressure against the poor; it also cites 7:32 that lawful enjoyment is permitted. Bursevi quotes ascetic remembrance of death. Ibn Ashur and Study Quran warn against mistaking status for favor."}]}
{"id": "18:46/q23", "question": "What inward meanings are drawn from the verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the enduring good is described as disciplined attachment, transformed adornment, or granted inward nearness.", "positions": [{"id": "18:46/q23/p1", "position": "The soul clings to worldly shares, while the spirit turns to reliance, certainty and worship.", "reasons": "Al-Sulami contrasts family, wealth and children with reliance, tranquility, trust and certainty. Al-Qushayri says heedless people adorn themselves with money and sons, the connected with works and certainty; status, praise and familiar attachments can also be worldly shares, even if results arrive later."}, {"id": "18:46/q23/p2", "position": "Escape from worldly ornament requires inward knowledge and love, and outward service and

 aspiration.", "reasons": "Al-Sulami says such people witness their King in nearness; Bursevi repeats the inward and outward program."}, {"id": "18:46/q23/p3", "position": "Enduring deeds are inward divine light or nearness.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayri reports lights of monotheism beyond veiling, divine qualities adorning hidden secrets and scenting heaven, or intimacy already granted from the unseen; al-Alusi reports lasting love, knowledge, sincere unity and turning away from others."}]}
{"id": "18:46/q24", "question": "How does this verse connect to its surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "Whether the link is to the local parable and resurrection sequence or to Qur'anic pairings elsewhere.", "positions": [{"id": "18:46/q24/p1", "position": "It concludes the image of worldly life vanishing like vegetation and prepares the resurrection scene.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the order 'enduring righteous' answers the wind-scattered plant of 18:45 and the mountain scene of the next verse recalls resurrection. Tabataba'i says the conclusion returns to the sura's opening claim about earthly adornment. Islahi says the next parable warns people blinded by worldly love. Kuran Yolu describes flourishing vegetation drying and scattering; Study Quran locates the long parable among the sura's three main narratives."}, {"id": "18:46/q24/p2", "position": "Other Qur'anic pairings present wealth and children as a linked trial or adornment.", "reasons": "Al-Farisi connects walad with wealth and children, citing 18:46, 64:15 and 64:14. Ibn Kathir cites 3:14 and 64:15; al-Qurtubi cites 64:15 and 64:14."}]}
{"id": "18:46/q25", "question": "What ancillary points about the preceding worldly-life parable are recorded?", "turns_on": "The notes give distinct lexical, theological, and grammatical comments on the adjacent parable.", "positions": [{"id": "18:46/q25/p1", "position": "Its vegetation becomes dry crumbling matter left after its brief beauty.", "reasons": "Abu Ubayda's Majaz glosses hashiman as dry crumbling plants and cites Labid's dry branches. Ibn Atiyya's fragment glosses a term as what a flood leaves, then turns to presentation in rows. Jishumi says the world resembles a briefly beautiful plant that yellows, crumbles and blows away, or water that never settles, remains unchanged, or always helps."}, {"id": "18:46/q25/p2", "position": "Earning livelihood serves as a divine trial and an occasion for reflection.", "reasons": "Jishumi records the question why people were not given enough to worship without earning; he answers that earning is worship, humbles people, displays mutual need, and teaches that God alone is self-sufficient."}, {"id": "18:46/q25/p3", "position": "A grammatical fragment parses hashiman as the predicate of 'became'.", "reasons": "Jishumi says al-nabat is its omitted subject."}]}
{"id": "18:46/q26", "question": "What ancillary literary examples appear in the collected notes?", "turns_on": "The collected literary notes discuss different examples.", "positions": [{"id": "18:46/q26/p1", "position": "Rain imagery treats hills as close to clouds and sky as a source of bounty.", "reasons": "Jurjani says hills, unlike valleys, lie nearer rain-bearing clouds; a veiled sky plausibly promises rain.
